# Changes Over Time in the Electrically Evoked Compound Action Potential (ECAP) Interphase Gap (IPG) Effect following Cochlear Implantation in Guinea Pigs

**Authors:** Kara C. Schvartz-Leyzac; Deborah J. Colesa; Christopher J. Buswinka; Donald L. Swiderski; Yehoash Raphael; Bryan E. Pfingst

**Affiliations:** 1Kresge Hearing Research Institute, Department of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery, University of Michigan, 1150 West Medical Center Drive, Ann Arbor, MI 48109-5616 | 2Hearing Rehabilitation Center, Department of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery, University of Michigan, 475 W. Market Place, Building 1, Suite A, Ann Arbor, MI 48108

## Abstract

The electrically-evoked compound action potential (ECAP) is correlated with spiral ganglion neuron (SGN) density in cochlear implanted animals. In a previous study, we showed that ECAP amplitude growth function (AGF) linear slopes for stimuli with a constant interphase gap (IPG) changed significantly over time following implantation. Related studies have also shown that 1) IPG sensitivity for ECAP measures (“IPG Effect”) is related to SGN density in animals and 2) the ECAP IPG Effect is related to speech recognition performance in humans with cochlear implants. The current study examined how the ECAP IPG Effect changed following cochlear implantation in four non-deafened guinea pigs with residual inner hair cells (IHCs) and 5 deafened, neurotrophin-treated guinea pigs. Simple impedances were measured on the same days as the ECAP measures. Generally, non-deafened implanted animals with higher SGN survival demonstrated higher ECAP AGF linear slope and peak amplitude values than the deafened, implanted guinea pigs. The ECAP IPG Effect for the AGF slopes and peak amplitudes was also larger in the hearing animals. The N1 latencies for a constant IPG were not different between groups, but the N1 latency IPG Effect was smaller in the non-deafened, implanted animals. Similar to previously reported results, ECAP measures using a fixed or changing IPG required as many as three months after implantation before a stable point could be calculated, but this was dependent on the animal and condition. For all ECAP measures most animals showed greater variance in the first 30 days post-implantation. Post-implantation changes in ECAPs and impedances were not correlated with one another. Results from this study are helpful for estimating the mechanisms underlying ECAP characteristics and have implications for clinical application of the ECAP measures in long-term human cochlear implant recipients. Specifically, these measures could help to monitor neural health over a period of time, or during a time of stability these measures could be used to help select electrode sites for activation in clinical programming.

## Introduction

Growing evidence suggests that performance outcomes in cochlear-implanted humans are at least somewhat dependent on the condition of the spiral ganglion neuron (SGN) population in the implanted ear (DeVries et al., 2016; Kamakura et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2010; Scheperle, 2017; Schvartz-Leyzac et al., 2018; Seyyedi et al., 2014). These studies show that various attributes of electrically-evoked potentials (electrically-evoked compound action potentials/ECAP or electrically-evoked auditory brainstem response/EABR), which are known to reflect SGN density in acutely and chronically-implanted animals (Hall, 1990; Pfingst et al., 2015a; Pfingst et al., 2017; Ramekers et al., 2015a; Ramekers et al., 2015b; Ramekers et al., 2014; Shepherd et al., 1997; Smith et al., 1983), are related to sentence or phoneme recognition abilities in humans with cochlear implants (CIs). Specifically, results demonstrate that the ECAP amplitude (when measured moderate current level) correlates with vowel and consonant recognition performance (DeVries et al., 2016; Scheperle, 2017). A related study measured ECAPs in bilaterally-implanted CI listeners and measured how increasing the interphase-gap (IPG) of the biphasic pulse changed characteristics of the ECAP amplitude-growth function (AGF) (“IPG Effect”) (Schvartz-Leyzac et al., 2018). These results showed that the ear with a greater IPG Effect of the AGF linear slope was the ear with better speech recognition.

Most of the studies that have examined the relationship between SGN density and ECAP measures have used shorter-term deafened animal models. However, previous results from our lab using a long-term implanted guinea pig model in which guinea pigs were evaluated for up to 426 days post-implantation have shown that 1) the ECAP AGF slope and amplitude change over time following implantation and 2) the pattern of change over time is partly related to the condition of the auditory nerve as assessed after the slopes have stabilized (Pfingst et al., 2015a). Among the non-deafened, cochlear-implanted animals with high SGN densities, ECAP slopes and amplitudes were generally low immediately following implantation, then slowly increased over time before reaching a period of relatively stable levels. Among deafened animals with poorer SGN densities, ECAP slopes and amplitude values also were low immediately following implantation but frequently remained largely unchanged for the duration of the experiment. In some animals, responses did not reach stability for nearly 100 days post-implantation. While the underlying causes of ECAP changes over time are not known, we hypothesized that in the implant only animals, ECAP changes reflect sequelae of CI insertion trauma and could represent changes associated with an inflammatory process (Pfingst et al., 2015a). In the deafened and implanted animals, these responses likely represent degeneration of cochlear structures (e.g., hair cells and/or SGNs) due to the deafening treatment, implantation, or natural aging.

Logically, variables other than SGN density (e.g., electrode location and factors that influence impedance) might also influence ECAP measures. The ECAP IPG Effect has been recently explored as an assessment of SGN density and/or function that might be less dependent on non-neural factors (Prado-Guitierrez et al., 2006; Ramekers et al., 2014; Schvartz-Leyzac et al., 2018). In humans, it has been shown that simple impedance values and ECAP responses using a constant IPG are correlated within an electrode array for some subjects; however, the same pattern was not present when examining the ECAP IPG Effect and impedance measures (Scheperle, 2017; Schvartz-Leyzac et al., 2016). While the underlying contributions to simple impedance measures are not yet clear, it is possible that these measures reflect attributes of the fibrous tissue or other biological material surrounding or adhering to the electrodes (Duan et al., 2004; Wilk et al., 2016). These factors probably change over time following cochlear implantation (Chen et al., 2013), and might help to account for some of the ECAP changes observed by Pfingst et al. (2015a) following CI insertion.

Taken together, data in both animals and humans as reviewed above suggest that there is potential to use ECAP measures to 1) assess and/or monitor neural status in cochlear-implanted humans and 2) guide modification of CI programming or processing strategies in order to maximize performance outcomes. Previous studies have used a ‘site-selection’ approach by which specific channels are chosen for activation or deactivation based on a psychophysical measure of performance or electrode location (Bierer et al., 2016; Garadat et al., 2013). Theoretically, ECAP measures also could be used in a site-selection approach, given that they reflect neural status adjacent to the implanted electrodes and show a relationship with speech recognition performance in CI users. As mentioned previously, the ECAP IPG Effect in particular was shown to be a promising measure for human clinical application (Schvartz-Leyzac et al., 2018). However, in order for such an approach to be successful it is important to understand the stability of this measure in a long-term, chronically implanted model akin to cochlear implantation in humans.

The primary aim of the current project was to assess how ECAP IPG characteristics, previously shown to be correlated with neural density in acute and shorter-term implanted animal models (Prado-Guitierrez et al., 2006; Ramekers et al., 2015b; Ramekers et al., 2014), change following cochlear implantation in a long-term, chronically implanted model. Specifically, the current study examined how three measures of the ECAP response: the ECAP AGF linear slope, peak amplitude, and N1 latency and the IPG Effect for each ECAP characteristic changed following implantation. It is important to examine all three measures in order to better understand how they can best be applied in a cochlear implanted human. For example, the AGF linear slope measure is sometimes difficult to accurately obtain for some electrodes in humans due to loudness discomfort or compliance issues resulting in a limited dynamic range (Schvartz-Leyzac et al., 2016). However, in these individuals the peak amplitude and N1 latency measures might still be valid and useful.

We hypothesized that, in parallel with previous results (Pfingst et al., 2015a), cochlear implanted guinea pigs with healthier cochlear anatomy would show larger ECAP IPG Effects that improve or recover post-implantation and reach a relative point of stability, while animals with less healthy anatomy would show smaller IPG Effects but also require more time to achieve a stable response. For comparison, we also considered changes over time for the three ECAP responses to stimuli with a fixed IPG. Finally, we examined how simple impedance measures changed following cochlear implantation, and determined whether or not they were correlated with changes observed in the ECAP measures from the same ears.

## Methods

### Subjects and overview

Methods reported here are similar, but not completely identical, to those reported in previous publications from this laboratory (Pfingst et al., 2015a; Pfingst et al., 2017). The animals used in these experiments were specific pathogen free (SPF) pigmented guinea pigs that were chronically implanted (161 days – 463 days) with a CI. Following implantation, ECAPs and impedances were measured until completion of all experiments and then animals were euthanized and histological analyses were performed. Some of the guinea pigs reported in the current study have been used in other experiments previously-published or in-progress. Only ECAP, impedance, and histological data are reported here. Only one animal (580L1) reported in the current study was also reported in Pfingst et al (2015a).

Animals used for these studies were bred and maintained by the Unit for Laboratory Animal Medicine at the University of Michigan. The animal-use protocol was reviewed and approved by the University of Michigan Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee.

This experiment utilized nine guinea pigs (Table I): four that received an implant in a normal-hearing cochlea (Hearing) and five that were deafened then given neurotrophin treatment to help preserve some neural function (Deafened). Deafening and implantation procedures were similar to those reported previously (Pfingst et al., 2015a; Pfingst et al., 2017). In the Hearing group, there was typically minimal loss of cochlear structures, which resulted in good hearing preservation and SGN survival the region of the CI (Kang et al., 2010; Pfingst et al., 2011; Pfingst et al., 2017; Pfingst et al., 2015b). Animals in the Deafened group underwent gene therapy treatment with one of two viral vectors with gene inserts (AAV.Ntf3, or AAV.Ntf3/BDNF; see Table I) following the deafening procedure. Note that the gene therapy treatment was not a variable of interest in this study, but was simply used to create a group of animals with heterogeneous SGN density patterns. A previous study in our lab showed that these gene therapy treatments help to protect the SGN from degeneration in deafened ears and result in higher SGN density in long-term implanted animals when compared to deafened and non-treated ears (Pfingst et al., 2017). However, animals that are deafened and treated with similar gene therapies typically have poorer cochlear health and lower SGN densities than animals that were not deafened prior to cochlear implantation (Pfingst et al., 2017). Details for deafening, inoculation, and implantation procedures for all groups are described below.

### Deafening, Inoculation and Implantation Procedures

Deafening procedures were consistent with previous experiments in our lab (Pfingst et al., 2015a; Pfingst et al., 2011; Pfingst et al., 2017). All animals were anesthetized with ketamine (40 mg/kg) and xylazine (10 mg/kg) and placed on a heating pad. A post-auricular incision was made, the temporal bone was exposed by blunt dissection, and the bulla was opened. In the Deafened group, animals were deafened by drilling a small cochleostomy in the basal turn of the cochlea approximately 0.7 mm apical to the round window using a hand drill. Bone dust and debris were removed from the area around the cochleostomy using a cotton pledget. Through this cochleostomy, neomycin sulfate (10 μl; 5% w/v) was slowly injected into the scala tympani (5 μl/min) using a cannula and an infusion pump. The infusion cannula was left in place for 20 minutes, and then removed. A drop of Healon (Hyaluronic acid; 10 mg/mL; Abbott Medical Optics, Inc., Santa Ana, CA) was placed on the cochleostomy to promote penetration of administered substances through membranes, and then using a new cannula with the infusion pump, 5 μl of AAV vector (Table I) were infused into the scala tympani at a rate of 1 μl/min. After the inoculation, the cannula was removed and the cochleostomy was either temporarily covered with a piece of muscle and allowed to sit for 30 minutes before insertion of the CI; or the cochleostomy was sealed with a piece of muscle and the bulla closed with Durelon and left for at least two weeks before cochlear implantation.

The CI in all animals was inserted through a cochleostomy which was either created at the time of implant insertion (Hearing group) or was created previously for neomycin and neurotrophin treatment (described above) then re-opened and enlarged with a diamond bur (Deafened group). An eight-electrode scala tympani implant was partially or fully inserted through the cochleostomy to the point of first resistance resulting in five to eight intracochlear electrodes. Note that all electrodes were located in the basal turn of the scala tympani. The implant was secured to the bulla with a silk suture, the bulla opening was then sealed with Durelon cement and the incision was closed.

Anchor screws were placed at three points around bregma and used to secure a small inverted bolt (specified as the “anchor bolt”) on which the connector that interfaced with the stimulator would be mounted; this anchor bolt was also used for the ECAP stimulating ground. An additional screw was placed at the midline, 1 cm caudal to bregma (specified as the “vertex screw”) and used for the ECAP recording ground.

### Cochlear Implants

The CIs (manufactured by Cochlear Corporation) consisted of either 8 full-band electrodes encircling a silicone rubber carrier (Standard 8-band implants) or 8 half-band electrodes on a silicone rubber carrier (HL8 implants) (Table I). The implant used in a given animal was based on what was available from the manufacturer at the time of implantation. All electrodes were spaced at approximately 0.75 mm center to center. For the full-band implants, the diameter of the implant near its apical end was 0.4 mm, so that it filled the majority of the scala tympani at about 4.5 mm from the cochleostomy and could not be safely inserted further due to the rapidly decreasing diameter of the scala tympani apical to that point, and implant insertion depth averaged around 4.2 mm. For the half-band implants, the diameter of the implant near its apical end was 0.20 mm and tapered so this implant was able to be inserted much deeper; on average around 5.5 mm. The primary electrode used for stimulation was the second most apical electrode (Electrode 2 in Fig. 1), which was located an average of 2.9 mm apical to the cochleostomy (approximately the 17 kHz region) for the banded implants and 5.5 mm apical to the cochleostomy (approximately the 8.5 kHz region) for the half-banded implants (Greenwood, 1990). In both implant designs, the primary electrode typically sat close to the modiolar wall. Figure 1 shows a midmodiolar section of a guinea pig cochlea with the profiles used for data analysis labeled “A” through “F”. The primary stimulating electrode for the banded implants was located in Profile A and for the half-banded implants the primary electrode was located in Profile B.

### Electrically-Evoked Compound Action Potential (ECAP) Amplitude-Growth Functions

ECAP AGFs were recorded in awake guinea pigs while the animals were standing in a test cage. Stimulation and recording for ECAPs utilized a MED-EL Pulsar CI100 receiver/stimulator connected to the implant through a percutaneous electrical connector. The receiver/stimulator was connected to a standard PC via a Research Interface Box (RIB II; University of Innsbruck). Measurement parameters were controlled using custom software developed in MATLAB (MATLAB, 2010a). Monopolar electrode configurations were used for stimulation and recording. The default protocol for this study was to stimulate the second most apical electrode in the CI (Electrode 2 in Fig. 1) and record from the adjacent, more basal, electrode (Electrode 3). The stimulating ground was the anchor bolt and the ECAP-recording ground was the vertex screw. The stimulus level was measured in current units (cu) where 1 cu was approximately equivalent to 1 microampere (μA).

The stimulus for ECAP recordings was a biphasic pulse, with 45 μs phase duration and 2.1 μs or 30 μs inter-phase gap (IPG). Pulses were delivered at 50 pps for 20 iterations. The recording amplifier was blanked for 213 μs following electrical pulse onset to reduce saturation artefacts. Prior to recording the ECAP on each day, the maximum stimulus level (MSL) that could be used for each stimulation site was determined. The MSL was based on observed facial twitch or pinna movement. The MSL for the ECAP experiments was typically set 10 to 20 cu below the current level which evoked a non-auditory response. To obtain an ECAP AGF, the program selected stimulus levels at 15 amplitudes evenly spaced from zero to the MSL and the order of presentation of the stimulus levels was permuted (8 1 9 2 10 15 5 6 14 13 12 7 3 4 11).

For every amplitude step, responses to an anodic leading biphasic pulse and a cathodic leading biphasic pulse were averaged to reduce stimulation artifacts and the response in the absence of stimulation was recorded and subtracted from this average to reduce non-stimulus related effects like switch-on artifacts. The resulting waveforms obtained for each of the 15 amplitude steps were plotted and analyzed using a custom-made MATLAB (MATLAB, 2010a) program. This program picked all negative peaks and positive peaks, which were then verified by visual inspection of the waveforms. The N1 to P2 amplitudes in μV were plotted against stimulus current in μA to obtain input-output amplitude-growth functions (AGFs).

For the AGF slope calculation, MATLAB (MATLAB, 2017) was used to calculate linear regression fits using a custom method. It was observed that the majority of AGFs were linear; however there were a small number of cases which demonstrated nonlinearity. In an effort to fit all data in the same way, the following method was used. All points below 100 μV (noise floor) were excluded from the fit function. The AGF was linearized by approximating the slope of the linear region using the ‘gradient’ function, and systematically removing the points that deviated by more than 20% of this slope. A linear regression model was fit to all of the remaining points. For a constant IPG, the peak amplitude was taken as the largest voltage response of the AGF, and the N1 latency was recorded at the stimulus level yielding this peak amplitude response. An example showing ECAP waveforms, AGF and the linear slope is shown for one animal (580L1) in Figure 2.

The IPG Effect for each ECAP measure (linear slope, peak amplitude or N1 latency) was calculated by subtracting the value obtained for the 2.1 μs IPG stimulus from that obtained for the 30 μs IPG stimulus. It should be noted that increasing the IPG often resulted in lower MSLs for all animals and therefore, the peak amplitude for the stimulus containing a 30 μs IPG was often obtained with a lower stimulus current level compared to the stimulus containing the 2.1 μs IPG. Therefore, the IPG Effects for the ECAP peak amplitude and N1 latency data were calculated using data obtained at equal current levels for the two IPG conditions, which was typically the MSL for the 30 μs IPG condition. The N1 latency values used were those observed at the stimulus levels corresponding to peak amplitudes, as defined above.

ECAP recording schedules varied slightly depending on the animal and the laboratory protocol at the time of data collection. ECAPs were recorded frequently throughout the first 90 days after implantation and monthly thereafter. Then, one final ECAP was recorded on or close to the day that the animal was euthanized.

### Impedance measures

Prior to ECAP recording sessions, the impedances of all the electrodes were measured using a custom-built impedance meter. Impedances were measured with a 1 kHz sinusoidal test current at 1 μA. Impedances were measured relative to a ground ball located in the neck muscle. In cases where this ground was broken, the anchor bolt was used. Impedances were used to confirm the function of each electrode used in the ECAP recordings. Only impedances from the primary intracochlear stimulating electrode and recorded on the same days as the ECAP recordings (+/− 1 day) are reported in this manuscript.

### Histology

After collection of all functional data was complete, animals were euthanized and perfused intravascularly with 4% paraformaldehyde. Temporal bones were extracted with the implant remaining in place in the implanted ear. For seven implanted ears, bone was carefully removed from the lateral wall of the cochlea, without prior decalcification, to permit the dissection of the cochleae for whole mounts. The location of the primary electrode was noted when it was revealed during the dissection, then the implant was removed and the dissection of the organ of Corti was completed. Then, the modiolus was removed from the temporal bone, decalcified in 5% EDTA with 0.25% glutaraldehyde, and prepared for sectioning. For the other two implanted ears, temporal bones were decalcified in 5% EDTA with 0.25% glutaraldehyde for 3 to 6 months until the bone was soft. As decalcification proceeded, softened bone was removed periodically to aid visualization of the implant electrodes. When the location of the primary stimulation electrode (Electrode 2) could be determined, the cochlear wall was marked at that location and the distance from the round window was noted, then the implant was gently removed. When decalcification was complete, the temporal bones were prepared for sectioning as described below.

To visualize hair-cells in whole mounts of the organ of Corti, tissue samples were permeablized with 0.3% Triton X-100 (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO) in phosphate buffered saline (PBS) for 1 hour, then incubated with Alexa Fluor® 594 phalloidin (Molecular Probes), diluted 1:400 in PBS for 30 minutes to label F-actin. Then, the tissues were mounted on slides, and cover-slipped with Gel/Mount (Biomeda, Foster City, CA, USA). The specimens were observed with a Leica DMRB epi-fluorescence microscope (Leica, Eaton, PA, USA) and photographed with a CCD Cooled SPOT-RT digital camera (Diagnostic Instruments, Sterling Heights, MI). Inner hair cells (IHCs) were counted in these images.

Tissues to be sectioned (whole cochleae or modioli) were embedded in JB-4 (Electron Microscopy Sciences, Hatfield, PA, USA) and sectioned with glass knives to obtain 3 μm thick sections in a near-midmodiolar plane. Using the notes and/or marks described above, the specimens were oriented to be sectioned parallel to the mid-modiolar plane passing through the estimated position of the primary stimulating electrode. Approximately 45 sections were collected per cochlea, beginning in that mid-modiolar plane.

The first section chosen for analysis was usually the section closest to the location of the primary stimulated electrode. If that section was damaged, the next closest section was used. Four other sections were then selected at intervals separated by a minimum of 6 sections (~18 μm) in order to prevent counting a cell more than once. The near-midmodiolar sections used for SGN counts were stained with toluidine blue. The specimens were observed and photographed using the Leica DMRB microscope and SPOT-RT digital camera, above. The cross-sectional area within Rosenthal’s canal containing SGN cell bodies was determined using ImageJ software and the cell bodies in each of the 5 selected sections were counted. Density of SGNs was calculated by dividing the number of cells counted by this cross-sectional area. Only cells with diameters of 12 to 25 μm and nuclei of 5 to 9 μm or more in diameter were considered. Of these cells, only healthy-appearing cells were counted; cells that had a poorly defined cell membrane or that appeared to be shrunken or atrophying were not counted. For ears that were decalcified and sectioned whole, IHC survival was estimated by counting the number of IHCs in each profile. To avoid counting the same hair cell in two sections, IHCs were only counted if both the nucleus and stereocilia were visible. The percentage of IHCs remaining in the whole mount sections and cross-sectional profiles of the organ of Corti, and the SGN densities in cross-sectional profiles of Rosenthal’s canal for the basal three half-turns of the cochlea (the areas occupied by the implant and just apical to the implant) are reported in Table I.

### Analysis

We calculated the day stability was reached for ECAP measures using a modified method of one previously described by Su and colleagues (Su et al., 2008) who determined behavioral psychophysical threshold stability by examining the standard deviation in windowed increments (5 time points), then confirming stability with a linear regression analysis. Briefly, the first step involved calculating the coefficient of variation [COV(standard deviation/mean)] in windowed increments (5 consecutive testing days). An ECAP response was considered ‘stable’ if the COV in a given time series window varied by a ratio of 0.10 or less. If the COV was equal to or less than the cut-off value (0.10 ratio), then step two involved fitting those same five values with a linear regression to determine if the slope of the line was significantly different from zero. A non-significant finding was indicative of a stable response over time. In order to confirm a relative stability point when compared to the remainder of time points for each animal and measure, we performed step three which consisted of a second linear regression analysis on all remaining data points for the duration of test days until the day when the animal was euthanized. Again, if the slope was not significantly different from zero, then the stability point was confirmed. Otherwise, if the slope of all remaining data points was positive or negative, then this was an indication that the ECAP measure was continuing to either increase or decrease over time. In this case, the stability point calculation was repeated but using the next window of five testing days (step two was repeated), followed by step three until the regression analysis was non-significant

It should be noted that because the IPG Effect is simply the difference between two ECAP measures using two IPG durations, it is inherently more variable than the ECAP recordings measured using a fixed IPG. Therefore, in order to adequately compare COVs for ECAPs measured with a fixed IPG and the ECAP IPG Effect, the mean values (denominator) were equal for both COV calculations. Specifically, the mean values for each windowed time series was calculated based on the fixed IPG data for each ECAP measure (e.g., linear slope, peak amplitude and N1 latency) which allowed for standardization across the COV measures. All data were analyzed using R Version 3.5.1 (RCoreTeam, 2018).

## Results

### Histology

Histological findings are reported in Table I. SGN density (cells/mm2) for The Hearing group ranged from 675 to 920 (Average = 799). All Hearing animals had IHCs present in the regions apical to the primarily stimulating electrode (Profiles B & C) but only 2 of the 4 (586L1 and 617L1) had IHCs in the area of the implant (Profile A). The SGN density for The Deafened group ranged from 63 to 450 cells/mm2 (Average = 247), and none of the animals had IHCs present in any region of the cochlea.

### Average ECAP responses for each animal and group

Overall, results show that the AGF slope and peak amplitude had greater ranges of values over time and larger mean values for animals in the Hearing compared to animals in the Deafened group (Figures 3 and 4). This pattern was also present for both the fixed 2.1 μs IPG and the IPG Effect conditions. For the N1 latency data, animals in the Hearing group showed a narrower range of ECAP values post-implantation compared to those in the Deafened group, but the average values over time were consistent across the two groups (Figure 5). Figures 3, 4 and 5 show jittered plots for each animal and group for ECAP AGF linear slope, peak amplitude and N1 latency, respectively. The symbols for each animal (Table I) are consistent throughout the manuscript. Each data point represents an ECAP response on a single test day following cochlear implantation. Levene’s test for equal variances showed that for each of the following analyses, equal variances were not observed. Therefore, the corrected values are reported below (Welch-Satterthwaite method to adjust the degrees of freedom).

When averaged across all data points over time for each animal, between group differences were also evident. For the ECAP AGF linear slopes (Figure 3), independent sample t-tests showed significant differences between the mean slope values for the Hearing and Deafened groups for the 2.1 μs IPG (t = 9.720, p<0.001) and IPG Effect (t=9.829, p<0.001) conditions, with the Hearing group demonstrating steeper slope and larger IPG Effect values. Similar between-group differences were observed for the ECAP peak amplitude data (Figure 4), and results show significantly larger peak amplitude values for 2.1 μs IPG conditions in the Hearing group compared to the Deafened group (t=23.853, p<0.001) and also for the peak amplitude IPG Effect (t=13.820, p<0.001). Results for the ECAP N1 latency data (Figure 5) show significant between-group differences for the N1 latency IPG Effect (t= −2.853, p<0.05) with the Hearing group exhibiting a smaller, average IPG Effect value across all testing days when compared to the Deafened group. However, between group differences were not significant for the N1 latency 2.1 μs IPG condition (t=1.451, p=0.149).

### Post-implantation changes in ECAP measures

Post-operative changes following cochlear implantation are shown for ECAP AGF linear slope, peak amplitude and N1 latency in Figures 6, 7, and 8, respectively. Figures A-B and C-D show data obtained using a 2.1 μs IPG and the IPG Effect, respectively. In order to better visualize the data, each animal’s data points were fit using the ‘loess’ (localized estimated scatterplot smoothing) function in R, and the resulting line is shown for each animal. Loess regression is a non-parametric method in which a least-squares regression approach is used in localized, moving windows. The number of data points used for each localized regression window can be adjusted (α between 0 and 1) using the ‘span’ argument, to create smaller or larger localized regressions, respectively. The alpha gives the proportion of observations that are used in each local regression. The graphs reflect the loess fitting with a ‘span’ value of 0.5. This analysis is not useful for statistical interpretation, instead, it is used to visually represent the trajectory of the functional data and how it changes following implantation. Unlike Figures 3,4,5, the x- and y-axis differ depending on animal group in order to adequately detail specific patterns of changes in each ECAP measure post-implantation.

Using methods cited above (see ‘Methods’), we attempted to calculate a stable point for each animal, for each ECAP measure for the 2.1 μs IPG and for the IPG Effect. Results are reported in Table II (2.1 μs IPG) and Table III (IPG Effect). These tables also provide average values across each group. In nearly all cases for which a stable period could be calculated for the 2.1 μs IPG condition (Table II), stability was achieved within the first 100 days post-implantation. Table III shows stabilization points for the ECAP IPG Effect and reveals that all animals achieved a stable response prior to 100 days, at least based on data for which a stability point could be accurately assessed. Within the 2.1 μs IPG and IPG Effect measures, there did not appear to be a significant effect of animal group. We performed independent t-tests in order to better assess this observation and there was no significant difference between groups for the day at which a stable response was calculated, within each ECAP measure (p>0.05). However, these results should be interpreted with some caution given that relatively few data points (2–4) were available within each group.

Overall, it appeared that the average number of days required to reach a stable response was fewer for the IPG Effect compared to data obtained using a constant 2.1 μs IPG. Independent t-tests were conducted using data collapsed across animal group. Results showed that the average peak amplitude stabilization point for 2.1 μs IPG condition was longer (89.6 days) compared to that of the peak amplitude IPG Effect (29.5 days) (t=3.01, p<0.05). Neither of the other comparisons (linear slope or N1 latency) was statistically significant. These conclusions should be interpreted with some caution given the limited data points available for the analyses.

Generally, Groups 1 and 2 exhibited different patterns of ECAP results over time post-implantation. For the Hearing group, the AGF slopes and peak amplitudes were lowest in the period shortly after implantation and then increased with time post-implantation; this was true for both the 2.1 μs IPG and the IPG Effect (Figures 6 and 7). For the Deafened group, the ECAP slope and peak amplitude values were generally lower than for the Hearing group soon after implantation and then either remained unchanged or decreased with longer durations post-implantation. The one exception in the Deafened group was animal 518R1 which showed a pattern similar to that for the Hearing group animals for the slopes and peak amplitude measures for the fixed (2.1 μs) IPG condition. Although not certain, it is possible that in this animal the neurotrophin treatment was more successful, and therefore the ECAP pattern of responses over time were similar to those in the Hearing group.

For the ECAP N1 latency, between-group differences were less clear (Figure 8). There did not appear to be any uniform pattern observed over time post-implantation as described previously for Figures 6 (linear slope) and 7 (peak amplitude). Results from Figure 5 suggest that there was overall less variability over time among animals in the Hearing group for the ECAP N1 latency measures compared to those for animals in the Deafened group; however, it appears from data shown in Figure 8 that the pattern of change for the N1 latency values and the N1 latency IPG Effect post-implantation was not uniform across all animals.

Next, we examined the COV for each ECAP measure for specific periods of time post-implantation. Specifically, the COV was calculated for each of the following time periods: 0–30 days, >30–100 days, and >100 days. The specific days for each animal were approximate as not all animals had responses measured on the exact end points of the time windows. These results are displayed in Figure 9 (A–F) and each plot shows the average COV for each time period, averaged across animals in each group. Results were further analyzed using the ‘cvequality’ (Version 0.1.3) (Marwick et al., 2019) package in R, and the ‘asymptotic test’ function (Feltz et al., 1996) to determine if COVs are significantly different for each group, as a function of post-time implantation. This analysis results in a single coefficient value (t-value), which indicates a significant difference between the three time periods but does not provide post-hoc analysis to define the specific differences. Note that these results should be interpreted with caution due to the limited number of subjects/samples presented in the current study.

Results show a fairly clear pattern (Figure 9), with the greatest variance observed soon after implantation (0–30 days). Statistical analysis using ‘cvequality’ revealed that for ECAP AGF linear slope, the COVs were significantly different between the time intervals within the Hearing group (t=6.567, p<0.05) and the Deafened group (t=5.64, p< 0.05). The same pattern of results was true for the ECAP AGF peak amplitude analysis in the Hearing group (t=10.60, p< 0.01) and the Deafened group (t=57.43, p<0.001), as well as for the N1 latency data in the Hearing group (t=7.57, t<0.05) and the Deafened group (t=29.11, p<0.001). For the AGF linear slope IPG Effect, result shown in Figure 9 suggest greater variability soon after implantation, but this difference was not statistically significant for either group (Hearing: t=4.57, p=0.10; Deafened: t=2.61, p=0.27). For the AGF peak amplitude IPG Effect, results showed that there was a significant difference between time periods for the Deafened group (t = 22.83, p<0.001), but not for the Hearing group (t=2.83, p=0.24). Analysis of the N1 latency IPG Effect data shows that, for each condition, the COV does significantly differ as a function of time post-implantation for the Deafened group (t=31.01, p<0.01) but not for the Hearing group (t=1.45, p=0.48).

It is important to note that this time-windowed analysis and interpretation do not conflict with data displayed in Figures 3,4,5 and interpretation of those data. The time-windowed analysis does show that, generally for each windowed increment, variability was larger in the Deafened group animals, while it was shown in Figures 3 and 4 that generally The Hearing group animals showed greater variability in responses over the duration of implantation. The difference between these two analyses is that the time-windowed increments analysis is a variance measure based on the average response during a specific time period (Figure 9) and Figures 3,4,5 show the raw ECAP values over the entire range of implantation. Because the ECAP values (peak amplitude and linear slope) were generally lower for The Deafened group animals, this affected the COV.

### Relationship between post-operative simple impedance and ECAP measures

Simple impedance measures for Groups 1 and 2 are shown in Figures 10. In order to better understand if post-operative factors that influence changes in simple impedances and ECAP measures are similar, Pearson’s pairwise correlation analyses were performed between simple impedance and ECAP measures within each animal. The resulting correlational matrix is shown in Table IV. Bonferroni correction was applied based on the number of comparison within each animal (0.05/6 = p<0.008). Correlation values shown in bold with asterisk in Table IV are significant based on the adjusted significance level of p<0.008. Generally, variances in simple impedance post-implantation were not correlated with changes in ECAP measures over time for either the 2.1 μs IPG or the IPG Effect conditions. A positive correlation was observed in 6/27 comparisons for the 2.1 μs IPG; only two significant correlations were observed for the ECAP IPG Effect conditions. These results suggest that different underlying factors are the main contributors to post-implantation changes in simple impedance versus ECAP measures.

## Discussion

The results of the present study are an extension of findings published by Pfingst and colleagues (Pfingst et al., 2015a) who reported on post-implantation changes on ECAP AGF linear slope and maximum acceptable stimulation level (i.e., threshold for eliciting a facial or pinna twitch) in cochlear-implanted guinea pigs. Here, we also report the AGF linear slope as well as the peak amplitude, N1 latency and the IPG Effect for each of these measures. Each of these measures has been shown in previous studies to reflect neural density and/or health to some extent (Hall, 1990; Pfingst et al., 2017; Pfingst et al., 2015b; Ramekers et al., 2014) and subsequent studies in humans have shown that some suprathreshold ECAP measures are related to post-operative speech recognition outcomes in human CI recipients (DeVries et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2010; Scheperle, 2017; Schvartz-Leyzac et al., 2018). In particular, we were interested in the post-implantation changes for the IPG Effect for each ECAP measure, which we previously found to predict speech-in-noise understanding for a group of bilaterally-implanted CI recipients better than ECAP AGF slope and peak amplitude measured with a constant IPG (Schvartz-Leyzac et al., 2018).

### Comparison with previous findings and changes following implantation

In keeping with previous results, this current study found that ECAP linear slope values tend to be larger in animals with better SGN density and that this pattern largely holds true for the IPG Effect on ECAP linear slope and peak amplitude as well (Figure 3 and 4). These findings are generally consistent with other studies conducted using cochlear-implanted animals who were either acutely implanted or implanted for a shorter duration of time compared to the current study (Prado-Guitierrez et al., 2006; Ramekers et al., 2015b; Ramekers et al., 2014). In keeping with results reported by Ramkers et al (Ramekers et al., 2015b; Ramekers et al., 2014), this study found that animals with higher SGN densities also showed ECAP IPG Effects for AGF slopes that were larger when compared to animals with lower SGN densities. Conversely, the present study also showed that animals with higher SGN densities demonstrated larger ECAP IPG Effects for peak amplitudes, whereas the opposite was reported by Ramekers and colleagues. It is possible that these differences are due to dissimilar methodological approaches. Ramekers et al (Ramekers et al., 2014)used a normalized amplitude measure to asses the IPG effect, and therefore it is not possible to make a direct comparsion with the results obtained in this study.

Also in agreement with Pfingst et al (2015a), ECAP AGF linear slopes for a constant IPG changed following implantation and the pattern of change was dependent on the health of the cochlea as assessed by SGN density at the end of the experiment. In non-deafened ears (Hearing group) we also found that the ECAP linear slopes and peak amplitudes were low soon after implantation and then increased over time. In deafened, implanted animals with poorer SGN densities, those ECAP responses were generally poor soon after implantation and remained small or were reduced further in value with increased duration of implantation. It does appear that two of the animals, 571L1 and 567L1 had slightly different patterns, at least for the 2.1 μs IPG data for linear slope and peak amplitude (Figures 6 and 7). In these two animals, values were somewhat higher and then decreased to levels equivalent to the remaining three animals in the Deafened group. This difference could be attributed to implant type, deafening treatment, or both of these factors. However, even the initial values are low compared to animals in the Hearing group (note the differences in the ordinate scale in the left and right panels).

### Comparing ECAP changes post implantation for a fixed and changing IPG

The patterns of ECAP responses over time within each group were similar when using a fixed IPG or when examining the IPG Effect (Figures 6,7,8). These results suggest at least a partial overlap of the underlying mechanisms driving the ECAP response with a constant IPG and the ECAP IPG Effect. However, it is likely that the mechanism for the ECAP IPG Effect is probably more complicated, involving not only dependence on the number of surviving neurons but also the morphology of those neurons. The IPG Effect theoretically depends on the excitatory phase of the biphasic pulse, which should be affected by the anatomy or health of the nerve (Rattay et al., 2001). It is quite possible that the change in IPG Effect observed over time following implantation is an indication of neural instability as a result of deafening/treatment (Deafened group) or insertion of the array (both groups).

This hypothesis is further supported by the N1 latency data measured using a fixed 2.1 μs IPG. The N1 latency responses for the 2.1 μs IPG stimulus showed a narrower range of responses post-implantation in the Hearing group versus the Deafened group; however, the average responses over all time points between the two groups were quite similar (Figure 5A and B). It is hypothesized that the latencies of the ECAP peaks, primarily N1, at high intensity levels are dependent upon the site of excitation along the neuron, with the site of excitation occurring at the peripheral process in the case of a healthy neuron with typical anatomy, but moving to the central axon in cases of significant neural degeneration (Rattay et al., 2001). Theoretically, this could result in shorter latency response in our Deafened animals. However, demyelination could slow the conduction velocity and increase N1 latency values (Long et al., 2018; Zhou et al., 1995). Thus, interpretation of latency data is ambiguous.

The fact that N1 latency values for 2.1 μs IPG stimuli showed greater relative stability post-implantation in the Hearing group versus the Deafened group would suggest that specific characteristics of neural health in the Hearing animals also remained relatively stable through the duration of testing (Figure 5A and 8A). In the Deafened group, the variability in N1 latencies most likely reflected changes in anatomy and biology following the deafening and neurotrophin treatment; specifically, the peripheral processes of the SGN neurons might be undergoing degeneration and demyelination after deafening (Long et al., 2018; Wise et al., 2017). Results showed that the remaining number of myelinated peripheral fibers is proportional to the cell bodies in deafened animals with and without neurotrophin treatment (Pfingst et al., 2011; Wise et al., 2005; Wise et al., 2017). However, changes in N1 latency should theoretically be affected by any degeneration of the peripheral process that might be occurring as the number of SGN fibers is decreasing. It should be noted that successful neurotrophin treatments in the deafened animal model have been shown to not only protect SGN cells from degeneration but also promote regrowth of non-myelinated peripheral neurites, although it is not proven that these project from the SGN cell bodies (Budenz et al., 2012; Budenz et al., 2015; Wise et al., 2010). Another consideration in Groups 1 and 2 is that the MSLs did change day-to-day and this could have theoretically affected the N1 latency if the maximum stimulation level was significantly reduced on a given day. However, this is unlikely to be the underlying cause of variances in The Deafened group N1 latencies given that the same pattern is not shown in Figure 4. In fact, Figure 4 (peak amplitude) shows that the opposite pattern is true: the Hearing animals show a broader range of responses post-implantation compared to the Deafened animals.

The N1 latency IPG Effect is even more difficult to interpret in the present paper given the fact that an alternating stimulus polarity was used for artifact reduction. The excitatory phase for a biphasic pulse has been shown to be either cathodic or anodic in electrical stimulation, and it has been hypothesized that the primary excitatory phase might depend on neural health, geometry of the electrode with respect to the stimulated neural population, species-specific anatomical differences or a combination of these factors (Macherey et al., 2008; Matsuoka et al., 2000; Miller et al., 1998; Rattay, 1999). The effect of IPG manipulation on the ECAP N1 latency might be minimal if the excitatory phase of the biphasic pulse is always the leading phase, regardless of polarity. Similar to N1 latency patterns for 2.1 μs IPG conditions (Figure 5A and 5B), the N1 latency IPG Effect in the Hearing group varied less over time compared to the the Deafened animals (Figure 5C and 5D; Figure 9F). It is logical that the variance in the Deafened group for the N1 latency IPG Effect stemmed from changes to neural anatomy and/or function following deafening and neurotrophin treatment, with similar reasoning as explained for the 2.1 μs IPG stimuli. It is hypothesized that the cathodic phase preferentially excites the peripheral process (i.e., healthy neural anatomy), while the anodic phase preferentially excites the cell body. Data in Figure 5C (Hearing) show a fairly constant IPG Effect on N1 latency over time perhaps suggesting more stable neural anatomy and preferential excitatory phase post-implantation. The Deafened animals (Figure 5D) show greater variability over time which suggests changing phase sensitivity post-implantation most likely caused by changes to neural anatomy and function.

### Comparison of ECAP and simple impedance measures

It was hypothesized in our previous study (Pfingst et al., 2015a) that post-operative changes in functional health measures (e.g., ECAPs) are associated with tissue damage and a subsequent inflammatory and healing process. Results in humans have shown substantial changes in impedance within the first hours and days following implantation (Chen et al., 2013), and changes post-implantation were also observed in the present study with cochlear implanted guinea pigs (Figure 10). In the present study, we examined whether the pattern of simple impedance changes over time correlated with post-operative changes in ECAP measures to test the hypothesis that the same underlying factors contributed to both measures. Results shown in Table IV did not support that hypothesis. While the factors that influence simple impedance measures in electrical stimulation of the auditory nerve are not well understood, it logical that tissue growth around the electrode, geometry of the electrode surface or properties of material adhering to the electrode surface might have affected impedance measures in this population (Duan et al., 2004; Franks et al., 2005; Tykocinski et al., 2001). Regardless, the present study suggests that the mechanisms underlying post-implantation changes in the ECAP data are not the same as those underlying the changes in impedance. Individual components that contribute to complex impedance measure might be more informative.

### Conclusions and implications for clinical use

The results of the present study have important implications for clinical application of ECAP measures, and in particular the IPG Effect. Previous studies have shown that enabling or disabling electrode sites based on functional performance can improve speech understanding in human CI recipients (Bierer et al., 2016; Garadat et al., 2013). Post-operative ECAP measures using a constant or changing IPG could be used in a similar manner, because both have been shown to be at least somewhat correlated with post-operative speech recognition scores (DeVries et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2010; Scheperle, 2017; Schvartz-Leyzac et al., 2018). Advantages of using the ECAP IPG Effect were noted in our previous findings (reviewed in Schvartz-Leyzac & Pfingst, 2018). The present study suggests that the ECAP IPG Effect reaches relative stability within seven weeks, on average, at least in the animal model. Further longitudinal data are needed in human CI recipients to better understand if the timeline is comparable to the guinea pig data reported here.

In the long run, it is important to understand the mechanisms contributing to the various ECAP measures discussed in this manuscript. Although their relationship to SGN density is well established, SGN density accounts for only about 50% of the across subject variance in these measures at best. Understanding the additional mechanisms is important for determining the optimal targets for biologically based therapies to improve conditions in the electrically stimulated cochlea and thus improve CI performance.
